evidence.source: CUHK Humanum, 漢語多功能字庫
evidence.field: 形義通解; Shuowen and Guangyun readings; dated use reports
evidence.text: The entry analyzes ordinary 好 as 女 plus 子 and lists proposed original motivations: woman’s beauty (Duan Yucai), mother–child affection (Liu Shengyou), and man–woman affection (Xu Kai and Chen Weizhan). Its editor favors the mother–child account partly because early 子 forms depict a child and are smaller than 女, while explicitly noting that cited early uses do not attest that proposed sense. The entry separately reports 好 in 婦好 as possibly 女 with phonetic 子, read 子 and representing the Shang 子 lineage name. It reports bronze examples for ‘good/beautiful’, ‘friendly’, and a loan use for 孝, and Warring States bamboo examples for ‘like’ and friendly relations. The listed examples do not establish a full semantic chain or an absolute date for the cited bronze vessels. Shuowen is recorded as 美也，从女、子; Guangyun fanqie 呼晧 and 呼到 occur in distinct tone categories.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 好

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; modern readings and senses
evidence.text: The official entry records the transmitted Shuowen analysis 从女、子 and both Mandarin readings hǎo and hào. It documents current senses including beautiful, good, friendly, intact, recovered, degree ‘very’, completion, ease, purpose and favorability before verbs; hào includes ‘love/like’. This lexical list records meanings and examples, not a dated semantic development.

evidence.text: The record indexes oracle-bone example 合集154, bronze example 集成00088, and a Shuowen form. The text corroborates that these interpretations are in circulation, but the database glyph images were not visually inspected and the record does not resolve the original motivation.

These are reconstructed readings of the whole character in two lexical uses. The 女-plus-子 ordinary graph analysis does not propose either component as phonetic.

The original motivation of ordinary 好 remains unresolved: the consulted accounts preserve mother–child affection, woman’s beauty, and man–woman affection proposals. CUHK explicitly notes that its cited early examples do not attest mother–child affection directly.

The cited sources report selected inscriptional and bamboo uses but do not establish the earliest ordinary lexical ‘good’ use, an absolute date for the bronze example, or a complete sequence connecting ‘good/beautiful’, ‘friendly’, and verbal ‘like’. Keep the Shang name 婦好 analytically separate; CUHK reports a distinct homograph/phonetic analysis for that name.
